utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Cross-examination by Mr. Stamp will now continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we show or have on the e-court P2 -- sorry, P425.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This, Mr. Jovanovic, is a document entitled"Proposals of Measures Such as Current Problems in Kosovo and Metohija." It's a photocopy of a booklet in our possession. Do you -- have you ever seen this document before, a document of this nature before from the Provincial Board of the SPS of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would the Provincial Board publish documents of this nature with this recommendations for solutions to the problems in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean would it publish such documents in public?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let's start with circulating among members of the party itself; would it do that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite usual for Provincial Boards to have their own documents and to distribute those in a written form to members of their bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see some handwriting on the top?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we move to page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recognise the handwriting on the top there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But I take it that you are familiar with documents like this, documents of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "this nature."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By proposals from, for example, the Provincial Board of the party in Kosovo in this format.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to confirm about the format. I don't remember the form and the appearance of those documents. I worked in the Main Board of the SPS. I can't confirm whether this was the form used at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we move to P810. This is -- these are some clips from a video. Sorry. The exhibit is P2909, and these are clips from a video which is P810, which I don't think is in evidence. What the clip which I propose to tender is P2909.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This -- sorry. Before we proceed, may I just indicate to the Court, it's a video or clips from a speech of Mr. Seselj made in 1989, and the -- it will be translated as it goes on, as it is played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying it's already part of the process?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Part of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. I don't think P810 has been tendered because it is a long video, but I think bits and pieces of it might have been. What we propose to do is to tender P2909, which are three small clips from what is in fact a long video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, proceed, please. Sorry, don't proceed. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't oppose this as a matter of principle. As usual, I am not inclined to oppose any moves by the OTP in an effort to prove something, but what I do oppose is bits of a document being tendered separately as a separate document. I think Mr. Stamp should tender the entire video, long as it may be, for us to see it. My fear is that some of these bits and excerpts might be taken out of context and might mislead us in some way. So that is the only remark that I would like to place on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it will be our responsibility to put before the Court the relevant part insofar as it is relevant to the issues before the Court. The Defence has the entire thing, and like any document they could use or proffer to the Court any part of that entire thing or, indeed, the whole thing, if they think it would benefit the Court from reviewing the whole thing. But I don't think we had a responsibility to -- to just throw, as it were, at the Court huge documents without trying to -- to extract the relevant parts for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There's one point. I believe Mr. Stamp said that P810 is in evidence. I don't believe it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He said it is not in evidence. If it says otherwise on the transcript, it's different from what he actually told us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what you propose is exactly what we've invited the parties to do so far as possible in the case, and you should proceed that way. It's for Mr. Fila, if he wishes, to explore other parts of the video or, indeed, even invite us to view the whole video, but we can deal with that in his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And finally, that which is our most vulnerable point: The Kosovo-Metohija issue, the issue of the Albanian separatist insurgency. The current military and police action in Kosovo and Metohija succeeded in eliminating the most extreme aspects of Albanian separatism and the repression of the Serbian population that lives there. "But I'm convinced that a lasting solution cannot be achieved in this way. In order to achieve the solution of Kosovo and Metohija issue, I propose a new colonisation of Kosovo and Metohija." "Applause."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we stop there. What I'm not sure of is if the witness hearing the video in the original Serb language? Is the witness hearing the video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you hear that, sir, in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to clip 2, please. Oh, could we continue clip 1. I'm told that clip 1 is not finished yet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "One should have no illusions about the possibility of returning those Serbs who have left Kosovo and Metohija, who have learned what it means to live with Albanians, a primitive and uncivilised people, as their next-door neighbours, who made it Belgrade and Serbia proper, found jobs there, built houses there, sent their children to school there, about the possibility of returning them to the nightmare of Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we now proceed to clip 2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... Whether it is moved to Pristina, Prizren, or some other place is not so important. What is important is that by moving the capital, the state institutions would be moved, all the state bodies and institutions, several hundred thousand government employees and members of their families would be moved. "In this way, the overall ethnic composition of the population of Kosovo and Metohija would change in a significant way, and it would mean a fresh financial injection, and the economic development of this depressed region would accelerate."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we continue, please, to clip 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "What I think the most important of all is this: I propose that all 360.000 Albanian immigrants who crossed over into Serbia and Yugoslavia from Albania after the 6th of April, 1941 urgently be sent back to Albania and be delivered to the UN High Commissioner for Refugees."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're a political scientist and a scholar. You told me earlier that you were not aware that Mr. Seselj was proposing the deportation of Albanians from Kosovo. Can I just ask you that a second time? As a professional scholar in your field, and as somebody who participated in the political life of your country for many years, were you not aware that Mr. Seselj was proposing the deportation of Albanians from Kosovo as the solution to the problems in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I object, Your Honour. I'm sorry. This is not my witness, but this is not correct representation of the evidence. Mr. Seselj was proposing to deport Albania Albanians from Kosovo who does not have proper papers to live in this country, and he continued the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't think that that sort of information in an objection is appropriate with the witness present in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we heard it on that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he will be able to deal with that himself, but the question is quite clear: "Were you not aware that Mr. Seselj was proposing the deportation of Albanians from Kosovo as the solution to the problems in Kosovo?" And that's perfectly consistent with what you've just said, and if the witness wants to explain more, that's for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to divide Albanians from Albania and Albanians from Kosovo. He mentioned Albanians from Albania, not from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the question should be composed in that way. Not just Albanians. We have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the whole matter's been so disrupted. This has been a quite inappropriate intervention without the witness being asked to leave the court. The whole point is now defeated in this piece of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the question in English, it may be different in Serbia, but in English, it is not suggested that these are Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But not either suggested that they were Albania Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It just says "Albanians."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. That should be specified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's wrong with --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is nothing --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because the question talked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please sit down. Your objection is repelled. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I think I will not go down that road any further. Can I just ask you this: You told us earlier that you agreed with Mr. Seselj that a lot of the Albanians in Kosovo were not Kosovo Albanians; they were migrants. Can I ask you this: Do you agree with Mr. Seselj that these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Allow --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- him to finish the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- that these so-called Albania Albanians should be sent back to Albania?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in your question, there is a statement that is factually untrue. I don't remember ever agreeing with that position you mentioned while I was answering your questions yesterday. So may that please be checked first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand what it is you say you don't ever remember agreeing. What is it you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My recollection is that he -- when I put to him that Mr. Seselj had said that many of the Albanians in Albania were migrants -- sorry, many of the Albanians in Kosovo were migrants from Albania and were not in fact Kosovar, he agreed that Mr. Seselj was correct on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you have a reference for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At 14223, line 14, 15, from line 15, question: "Are you not aware that Mr. Seselj claimed that there were hundreds of thousands of Albanians living in Kosovo who were not from Kosovo? Answer: "I am aware of that claim and that is a true fact."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, does that help you, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that definitely helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you now deal with the question that's been asked, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a well-known fact that, over several decades, people were crossing into Kosmet from Albania in a bid to flee from the horrifying conditions under Enver Hodja's regime, and that is how many Albanians from Albania arrived in Kosovo and Metohija. They were never properly registered. If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you would just deal with the question. I mean, do you agree with Mr. Seselj that those who were not Kosovo Albanians but migrants should be sent back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I do not agree that this should be done by force; but as any other country, I believe we should protect our position by dealing with those citizens who don't have proper papers, regular papers, as any country would through a regular procedure and send them back to their own home countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you aware of Mr. Seselj advocating this position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm aware of this position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, yesterday, you weren't aware of it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just seen the footage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Had you forgotten about it or was this new to you or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's new to me. I've just seen the recording, and I don't remember that statement originally being made or taped like this. And could I please have the year for this recording? I would really find that very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Counsel said "1989." Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. Just a minute. I think that yesterday the witness said that he was aware of Seselj making those statements. I will go back through the transcript myself to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help us on the transcript, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. My recollection is that he said that he did not -- was not aware, and it's at 14223. Question: "Are you aware that for" -- sorry, I beg your pardon. "Are you aware that Mr. Seselj had proposed expulsion of some Albanians from Kosovo." And he answered: "I'm not I wear of that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems to be clear enough, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'll check, Your Honour, but I think he said he knew about Seselj requesting that those people be expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That position that you just took, Witness, shall we say the status of these people that moved across the border and were living in Kosovo for decades should be regularised, you're saying not by force, but that position which you are saying is your position, was that a position which by the latter half of 1998 many senior persons in your party had begun to adopt, undertake? The same position that you just advocated here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember an official position by the SPS confirming that the Albanians who had crossed over into Kosmet illegally from Albania should be expelled, should be sent back by force, nor was that a subject that was ever discussed by the party, at least not as far as my knowledge goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it that your employment by the SPS as an expert was based not only on your political skills and training but also your world view, your political philosophy, then, could I say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One's own world view is one thing. The other thing is what your employer may or may not choose to adopt and include in their official documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, that is precisely the point. Some things were in official documents and some things were not. Well, I guess that's a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before you re-examine. Mr. Lukic, is there anything arising out of this that you think needs to be clarified from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just wanted to point out the differences in between the question and what Mr. Seselj said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I simply invite you in future to do it in a more subtle way. As it turns out, no damage was done in this instance, but it can be done because the result of the objection can be to alert the witness to a point that perhaps would not otherwise have occurred to him; and, therefore, if there's a risk of that, you should invite us to ask the witness to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please first have P425. This is an OTP document that was just shown a minute ago. Can we please have page 1 back on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You see what the Prosecutor warned you about? It says: "Crime at Pec, the 14th of December, 1998." Do you remember anything like this in Pec in the Panda Cafe, six Serbs being murdered there on that day? Teenagers, young Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that a bomb was thrown into that cafe and six young people were killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could be this be in reference to that crime, unless of course the claim is being made that the Serbs were simply killing themselves, because that was also something we heard?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's entirely possible that this note is in reference to that crime and the date is quite specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. Are you aware at all of the fact that Seselj gave all sorts of statements from the moment he became the president of the Radical Party? What sort of statements being made by him do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, this is a very long period and there were different statements. Some were very inflammatory. Of course, that does not mean that we, as a political party, accepted that what Mr. Seselj as the president of the Serb Radical Party said, especially when we were in coalition. As is well known, politicians say all sorts of things in public. So the Socialist Party of Serbia called Mr. Seselj and the Serb Radical Party "fascists," and Mr. Seselj and his party called our party "traitors." Nevertheless, we formed a coalition government in the interest of defending state and national interests. In the official positions of the government, and in terms of what the official authorities did, there is not a single act or a political position that would mean violently resolving the problem in Kosovo or taking any kind of forceful or illegal action against the overall population in this province of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw the footage, and the Prosecutor says that is in 1989. That's about ten years before the things for which we are sitting in this courtroom happened. If you saw this footage, well, is this some kind of a political party manifestation? Is it in the United Nations? What does this look like to you? Or should we play the footage for you again?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very thankless to comment on something that is taken out of context. That is the first matter I wish to refer to. Secondly, I did see the video clip but it's very blurred. Thirdly, on the basis of what is seen on the video clip, it is possible that he's speaking in front of a small number of people in a small office, and, obviously, this is a gathering of his political party or for promotion purposes. In terms of the setting, as far as we can see from the video clip, it is by no means official premises or public premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you remember that, in his public statements, Seselj insulted President Milosevic, his wife, his children, you, all of you? What were all the things he said? Don't hesitate. We have to see how serious statements made by such a specimen of the human race are.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj used very ugly and insulting expressions for our president, Slobodan Milosevic, and for his wife, calling her the "Red Witch," insulting his children. As for the arsenal of insults thrown at the Socialist Party of Serbia, it was wide-ranging. Most serious were these words about betraying state and national interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How did you betray state and national interests?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, it was said when the Dayton peace agreement was signed, he and his party opposed that, and they were in fierce opposition to that, to the Socialist Party of Serbia in that period. This was uttered not at some party gatherings but in an Official Note in parliament when the Serb Radical Party initiated proceedings to have the government replaced.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter did not hear Mr. Fila's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Dayton Accords have to do with peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina. May I answer? It is well-known that we practically accepted and supported all peace agreements that were being offered for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And he called that treason?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He called that treason.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was his characterisation of the Kumanovo agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb Radical Party and Mr. Seselj were against the Kumanovo agreement, and, practically, they boycotted the work of the Assembly then and they did not vote to support the Kumanovo agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something now, Mr. Jovanovic, because you got all these fabulous compliments from the Prosecutor that you were a political scientist, a scholar, that you were involved in the field of scholarly studies. When you said all of this what Seselj said about the Socialist Party of Serbia, that your president was insulted, his wife, the party, does that mean coalition when you -- do you accept all of that that is said by your coalition partners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We absolutely did not accept such positions. But when -- if political parties were to look at what they were saying about one another, then it would be very hard to form a coalition government in any country.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you accept his extremist views in relation to Kosovo or anything else, as the Prosecutor says, either in the documents or de facto or both?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not accept extremist views, not only of the Serb Radical Party but of any other party. We had a clearly defined policy based on a political solution by peaceful means with the full equality of all ethnic communities. We insisted on that to the very end, and this is contained in state documents. It is clear that in this way we suppressed the extremist views that did exist in the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to -- do you still have that? Oh, yes. Tab 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move to a different subject, there are a couple of issues to be clarified. Can you give me an example of Mr. Seselj's extremist views on Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is hard for me to remember now and to interpret some statements without being complete. In part of this video footage, we saw that he advocated a fast resolution of the Kosovo problem by radical means, but this was more rhetorical rather than being translated into any kind of concrete action. If I may, I would like to explain. We had formed a government with the Serb Radical Party; but at the same time, as regards Kosmet, we talked to those who attacked our country, killed our citizens, and carried out terrorist actions; that is to say, that the fact that we talked to the extremists does not mean that we accepted their positions and their policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you would answer my question, please, and give me an example of an extremist position taken by Mr. Seselj in relation to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right now I cannot remember a specific example and take it out of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of an extremist position he took when you were in coalition that your party did not accept, on any matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already mentioned the non-acceptance of the Kumanovo agreement. He had rejected that document, and they did not support it in parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And remind us of the date of the Kumanovo agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was sometime in March. It was sometime around the 75th day of the bombing if you start counting from the 24th of March. I do not recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what did that do to the coalition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Seselj left the coalition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's look at a situation where in the currency of the coalition Mr. Seselj adopted an extremist position which your party would not accept. Give me an example of him doing that on any subject at all. Take the world as your oyster.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll repeat it. Let's look at a situation where during the coalition Mr. Seselj adopted an extremist position which your party would not accept on any subject at all. It doesn't need to be confined to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were different examples related to legislation from the field of employment, the taxation system, the budget, but it is only natural that in a coalition one partner may propose something but the other partner doesn't have to support it necessarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, this is about extremist positions, not about normal political disagreement. Please confine your answer to an extremist position that Mr. Seselj has taken, something that is universally unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall any such statement now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So, in his political life, Mr. Seselj's activities and his positions were, in your opinion, all reasonable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not what I said. I said that I cannot remember any extremist positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm trying to be helpful. Did Mr. Seselj mention Mount Prokletija, and that you did not accept something in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a statement of that nature, that the Siptars should be sent to the other side of Mount Prokletija. Of course, we did not accept that or any other such positions, but it is hard for me to remember them now and to locate them in a time that would be relevant to a narrower area because there are many events and many things that were referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was a border mentioned that would not be in keeping with Dayton, Karlovac, Karlobag?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Seselj's standard statement that the western boundary should be along that line that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you accept that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we did not. We supported peace agreements for Croatia and for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your view, would these be examples of extremist views, what was referred to just now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are examples of extremist views that we did not accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you actually saying that after Dayton, during the coalition, the Serb Radical Party position was that the border had been wrongly defined and should be changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is such a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you were able to remain in coalition with a party that thought that the border should be changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We managed to, because we did not accept such a position, and it was not official state policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I can go on until tomorrow morning listing all of these positions, but these two will do. Now I would like to move on to something else. Please look at tab 12, 1D91. Please look at item 3. It says there that "competent state authorities will organise as soon as possible." Could you read it out now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, we'll have a look. It's hard for me to do everything at the same time. So tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think that if counsel proposes to ask questions about a document that I didn't ask questions about, then perhaps he should preface what he's doing by indicating how it arises in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How does that arise, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It says there that the "competent state authorities ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, there's been an intervention asking you to explain how this document can be explored on a matter that arises out of cross-examination. What is it that Mr. Stamp raised that you are dealing with by referring to this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now going to resolve that straight away. Sorry. I was dealing with something else. I didn't hear you. It has to do with the census, the population census. Look at what I'm talking about. Mr. Stamp raised the question of the Albanian population, the census, and so on. So that's it. I simply didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's all he wanted, an indication of the subject. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is stated there that the state organs would carry out a census under the supervision of the OSCE. Why was a census needed, and was it supposed to be carried out before the elections? That is why you need to look at item 4 as well, and to explain all of that to us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The census was needed because in Kosmet, in all the censuses that were carried out from 1948 and then 1953 and then 1961 and then 1971, and especially 1981, there were serious objections raised in terms of forging the results of these censuses. That is why we advocated having the census carried out under the auspices of the OSCE, so that, once and for all, there would be the most precise information possible about population numbers and the representation of different ethnic communities in Kosovo. In the very last document that the Prosecution showed me, in the English language, there is a reference to Albanians constituting 81 per cent of the population. The federal statistics office in the officially published study related to the census, in the methodological notes, it explicitly states that they tried to prevent a boycott of the census, that they contacted the Academy of Sciences of Kosovo and Metohija, that they contacted political parties in Kosovo and Metohija, and that they made certain reservations and set certain pre-conditions for their support of the census. Their conditions related to the following: "Mixed composition of the census teams that would visit households." That was accepted. "Bilingual census materials," which was also accepted. "Control and verification when processing the data," which was also accept. However, in spite of the fact that these positions were accepted, they boycotted the 1991 census. Now look at this. This is what statistics officially say: "We made an estimate on the basis of the data from 1981, and there is a serious suspicion that the data in 1981 were forged in the following way: The census was carried out without any kind of control by the provincial statistics office, and, abruptly, there was a disappearance of Roma and then the Turks from the statistics data; then Muslims, then Egyptians." You now have information from 1991 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you need all this information?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please control the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to judge what is necessary for your case, so please exercise control over his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It was my wish to establish why in that agreement you asked for the census to be carried out under OSCE supervision. Could you give a shorter answer? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first reason was to establish as objectively as possible facts related to population numbers and their ethnic composition. The second one was to prepare voting lists because elections were supposed to be held.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Interpreters did not hear Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within nine months' time, free and fair elections would be held for all organs in Kosovo and Metohija, and this document envisages that the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia called upon the OSCE to supervise these elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During the census, would only those who have proof of citizenship of the province of Serbia and Yugoslavia and so on be registered?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. What would be established would be the exact number of inhabitants according to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please look at tab 13 now. The same subject like the previous. This is an agreement dated the 15th of March, 1999. It's a Defence exhibit, 2D384. Please look at chapter 3. Does this envisage a census done jointly with the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here, there are three points stating that: "The competent state organs together with the OSCE will," it says here "as soon as possible, make it possible to contact an objective and free census which will ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question. If Mr. Fila wants more information, he'll ask you for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does that mean that the institutions in Kosovo and Metohija would be established in the manner proposed in this agreement, regardless of whether someone thought there were so many of those and so many of the other ones?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The institutions would be set up according to the results of the census which would be conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And would then all these claims about the numbers of Albanians, Serbs, and other groups then be superfluous if a census were carried out under the supervision and with the monitoring of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm convinced the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And would then, in your view, this topic be forever closed about the number of citizens of this or that ethnicity or religion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it would be closed for good, because passions are involved mere, but the results would be questions would be objective and acceptable to all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did our side ask for that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our side asked for that then, and our government is still insisting on it today because a census has not been conducted yet according to these criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And, finally, the Prosecutor and also His Honour the Presiding Judge dealt with the issue of confidence. The co-presidents, Mr. Vedrine and Cook, did they hand that document over to the Albanians? And you then said that you had no reason not to believe he did, because they gave you documents from the Albanians. I would like to delve a little deeper into this. How did you find out whether the other side, which was sending you these documents through Messrs. Vedrine and Cook, was receiving the documents? How did you come by this information?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their replies were conveyed by the negotiating troika. Ambassadors Hill, Mayorski, and the Albanian delegation stated publicly their attitude to the documents they received, and that's how we learned about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you assert with certainty that the Albanian side was familiar with all the attempts being made by our side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely sure that the Albanian side was acquainted with the contents of our document in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That concludes my -- my examination. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Jovanovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before proceeding to the next witness, let me raise one administrative matter. There is a motion before the Trial Chamber, at the instance of the accused Lukic, to bar the Prosecution from interviewing any of the Defence witnesses. The Chamber propose having a hearing on this to explore certain issues with the parties, but also to hear any further submissions that they wish to make. I'm giving you notice of this, at the moment, so that you can be prepared for it, because it may be fixed at very short notice. What we'll try to do is not intrude upon the sitting times for taking evidence, and there may be a measure of flexibility about the available time next week. So please be prepared for that at short notice. Your next witness now, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my next witness is Andreja Milosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to take this opportunity to thank Mr. Hannis for his great assistance in having Mr. Vasiljevic appear on videolink on the 29th. As you saw, I was right when I thought the right man had to be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Milosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Fila on behalf of Mr. Sainovic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like the witness to be given and bundle of exhibits, and for the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Give praise to the Prosecutor with one hand, Mr. Fila, and take the legs away from him with the other. Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, but I have given him a copy. Very Christian on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosavljevic, are you all right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, relatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You are the oldest witness who has been here to date, so we will understand that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, 71, that's quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm now asking myself whether you're the oldest in the courtroom though. We have never found out the answer to that question. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Defence is stronger there. Mr. Sep -- is quite old.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you please give us your full name, and then tell us about your career.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Andreja Milosavljevic. I was born in October 1936 in the municipality of Zagubica, Serbia. I completed primary school in my native Krpoljin, the secondary school in Petrovac Na Mlavi, and the Faculty of Law in Belgrade. I retired as a misdemeanors judge. I was also deputy president of a municipality. I was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, it is quite important to perhaps speak a little more slowly than you would normally do because everything has to be translated, and the interpreter has to have an opportunity of picking it all up. It's also helpful if you can just pause after the questions asked to allow that to be translated before you answer, so that we can develop a routine here which will ensure that everything is properly translated. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It's not on the record, Mr. Milosavljevic, so we will repeat. You say you graduated from the Faculty of Law. You were a misdemeanors judge. That's how far we've got. Then you were a secretary?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The secretary of the Municipal Assembly of Zagubica, the president of Zagubica municipality in several terms of office, director of the Jasenovac coal mine in Krpoljin, managing director of the cast factory in Zagubica, minister in the government of the Republic of Serbia, and president of the Committee for Establishing Damage from Natural Disasters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the level of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at republican level.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In what period of time were you a minister in the government of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a minister in the government of the Republic of Serbia tasked with development and reconstruction and promoting local self-management in the period from March 1994 to March 1998, throughout this term of office. I was also Minister of Religions in the period of September 1997 to the end of March 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And, in that period, did the government appoint you president of the Committee for Establishing Damage caused by Natural Disasters?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: When the government was appointed, I was -- from that time, I was president of the Commission for Establishing Damage Caused by Natural Disasters, and I was re-elected president of the commission in -- at the end of April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, did you go to Kosovo and Metohija before 1998?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As the director of the cast factory in Zagubica, in the 1980s, I would go to Janjevo, which is close to Pristina, to visit the Metalac factory, because we had similar programmes and similar production lines. I would go there to obtain raw materials, tools, and semi-finished products.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, you've been -- you've lived for quite a long time, so if we were to go through your entire CV, it would take a long time. So as minister?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As minister in charge of local self-administration, I often had occasion to go to Kosovo and Metohija in order to deal with important issues falling under the competence of the republic. These were issues of functioning, funding, the work of the administrative organs, and so on and so forth. I was especially tasked with establishing the reasons for the setting up of municipal councils in the municipalities where elections had not been held or had been held but were irregular, and then the government of the Republic of Serbia established municipal councils whose task was to replace the work of the Municipal Assembly and its Executive Committee. In these municipalities, the citizens did not turn up to vote, and that's why the organs were not elected. The government of the republic, in compliance with the Law on the Territorial Organisation of the Republic of Serbia and local self-administration and the provisions contained in Article 45 and 64(A) of this law, was duty-bound to set up these municipal councils so that the municipalities could continue to function. I can enumerate some municipalities, such as Glogovac, Decani, Stimlje, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this information we need to have?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but it's hard to stop him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And when you were president of the Commission for Repairing Damage from Natural Disasters, did you visit Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you hold any positions such as president of a management board at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1997, I was appointed president of the management board of one of the largest companies in Kosovo and Metohija, Feronikel from Glogovac, which employed 1.800 personnel, 85 per cent of whom were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And did this complex have any difficulties in doing business?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, when I put my question, look at your screen; and when you see the writing stopping, that's the time to start answering. I do the same. So did the Feronikel company, of which you were the president of the management board, run into difficulties, and how did it solve these?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely. Because it had great difficulties, there were frequent meetings of the management board with a view to finding adequate solutions. Tasks were handed out, new decisions had to be reached, debts had to be rescheduled. Production had to go on because the state was very interested in these products as almost a hundred per cent of our products were exported.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how was this solved?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, attempts were made to solve of it. All decisions were is made on time, funds were found, and the company continued working; although, there were problems there, averages and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you become involved in solving the problems of other producers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Trepca and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Can we, therefore, conclude that the conditions and problems in Kosovo and Metohija were something you were familiar with, quite well, in fact?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Quite well. Yes, I'd put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine. During your time in Kosovo, did you take part in any negotiations about Kosovo and Metohija as a member of the negotiating team led by Ratko Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, before you answer, look at 1D78.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can I ask my question first, please. 1D78. Can you tell us what this is about, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a statement made by the Information of Ministry of the government of the Republic of Serbia, saying that at its session, dated the 10th of March, 1998, the government appointed its representatives for talks with the leaders of the Albanian parties and associations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who were the members of this negotiating team?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the government, heading the delegation was Professor Ratko Markovic, and the delegation also comprised three of the government ministers: Minister Vico, Mr. Sedlak, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the reason for the cabinet deciding to send you there.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: We wanted to have a dialogue. The cabinet was in favour of that. It was in favour of using political means to deal with problems, because what depended on this were the human civil rights of all of those in Kosovo, as well as issues connected with the economic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note; could the speakers please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the constitution of Serbia was used as a framework for these talks, as well as international and European standards; the UN charter; the Paris charter of the OSCE; there was the Helsinki final act; and the framework convention of the Council of Europe on ethnic issues -- or rather, ethnic minorities, the protection of ethnic minorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you go there a number of times, and did any representatives of Albanian majority parties ever turn up at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did go a number of times with this delegation. I went to these talks, and as far as I remember, seven or eight times. Once the new cabinet had been set up, the new negotiating team was established and I was no longer a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the new cabinet was elected when?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Late March 1998. Albanian majority parties did not go to those meetings. Some other ethnic groups were represented: The Roma, the Gorani, and so on and so forth. We talked several times. We talked to whoever was there, but we went no further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What do you mean by that; "we went no further than that"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: What I mean is the majority parties of the Albanians would not turn up for these talks. We would just go there and then we would leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To what position were you appointed in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Early in June 1998, I was appointed coordinator of the state bodies in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Which state?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And your task was to do what?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: To coordinate the work of all state organs, state bodies, and to implement measures and any policies pursued by the government of the Republic of Serbia based on any enactments adopted, and so on and so forth. Already decrees adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To coordinate the work of all state bodies in Kosovo and Metohija, you say, and to work in line with which legal enactments?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The constitution and all the positive laws and any decrees adopted by the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The objective being what?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The objective was for all of the state bodies to work smoothly with no interruptions or irregularities and to have a normal life in Kosovo and Metohija, for life to go on as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now please go to exhibit -- or rather, a proposed Defence Exhibit, 2D136. Have you found it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you look at it carefully and slowly -- go through it slowly and tell me when I can start asking my questions.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Fire away.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you have a look, please, first?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No need. I know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The first document --

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The first document is a different document; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. What I have is the deputy Secretary-General, Mira Djurekovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Take it easy, please. Whose document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And this deputy General-Secretary, Mira Djurekovic, is informing you about what?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: About the fact that I was appointed coordinator of the work of state bodies in Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] - adopted by the prime minister of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- on the screen because it doesn't appear to be in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 2D356.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is in the bundle. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, please, can you wait until after I have finished asking my question, and then there's the interpretation, and then please steadily. We're in no hurry at all. This is not a sprinting competition, sir. Could you now please look at the next document. What does this document say?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: This document tells me that I am hereby appointed coordinator of the work of state organs or bodies of the Republic of Serbia in Kosovo and Metohija. It specifies my tasks. It says here that: "Andreja Milosavljevic shall coordinate the work of all state organs in Kosovo and Metohija, proceeding from their rights and duties as laid down in the constitution and the law. He shall be required to report directly to me on the work of these organs at least once a week."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who adopted this decision, and who is the person that you are supposed to be reporting to at least once a week? Can you please wait for the interpretation. Can you follow the interpretation on the transcript. Once the letters stop appearing, please start with your answer.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: This decision was adopted by the prime minister of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Mirko Marjanovic, in June, more specifically, the 3rd of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He so who are you supposed to be reporting to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: To him. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you go to our third document now. It reads "Republic of Serbia." So what's this about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a copy of a document that I received from most of the ministries, informing me about the responsibilities of the certain officials, certain persons, who it says would be in touch with me in situations where the minister himself was to remain in contact. In this specific case, there's the Ministry of Finance nominating three persons, or rather, the deputy Minister of Finance, Mr. Golic, and two assistants, one in charge of funding local self-administration and one in charge of matters regarding to the entire system.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that this was some sort of a pattern, a copy, a model, if you like, a model document. It is a model document, in a manner of speaking, but what exactly do you mean by that? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: What I mean is: I would receive information and reports from other ministries that were just like this. I mean, the substance was very much like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does this mean that all of the ministries were represented and all of the ministries were helping you along? Most of the ministries at least.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. I wasn't in touch with all of them, really, just those that were helpful in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This might be a convenient time for our break now that I've finished with this particular topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Milosavljevic, we have to break at this point for 20 minutes or so. The usher will show you where to go while we're out of court, so could you please accompany the usher from the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've been advised in the intervening time, there is a prospect that we will be sitting on Tuesday, and that will be a Tuesday afternoon sitting if it takes place. We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Milosavljevic, we spoke about your responsibility to report to Prime Minister Marjanovic at least once a week. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Let us talk about how long your responsibilities went on for. Until what time did you remain in your position of coordinator for the government of the Republic of Serbia in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I arrived in Kosovo and Metohija early in June 1998. I left the area on the 28th of September, 1998, on account of my illness. I attended the second extraordinary session of the national assembly of the Republic of Serbia, which considered the current situation, as well as the security and economic situation in Kosovo and Metohija. There was the report of the government of the Republic of Serbia on the measures taken to normalise the conditions in Kosovo and Metohija. I sat in the session until 1300 hours. I suddenly became very ill, and I had to be taken urgently to the hospital of Bezanijska Kosa, where after three or four days early in October I underwent surgery. I stayed in hospital for quite some time; therefore, as of the 28th of September, I had no further activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. It is based on this that we shall be limiting ourselves in our following set of questions. June, on the one hand, and the 28th of September, on the other, this is the period that we'll be discussing, sir. Can you now please look at a Defence document, 2D372. Please look at it slowly, gradually, and then I'll be asking you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You've looked at the letter; right? I'll ask you something about it. You have the document in front of you, don't you? I'll be pressing on now. We determined the period that you spent working hours as a coordinator. Now we want to know about the scope of your work, what your specific responsibilities were, what your work as coordinator of the government of the Republic of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija really comprised. Slowly, please. These are complex words.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: My work as coordinator in Kosovo and Metohija meant this: I was coordinating the work of the ministries of the Republic of Serbia, the head of district and the president -- the presidents of the municipalities, and also goes without saying worked with the special organs, such as the cadaster office, the revenue office, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. How many districts were there? How many heads of districts? How many municipalities and how many presidents of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: There's a total of five districts and five heads of districts in Kosovo and Metohija. Those were appointed by the government of the Republic of Serbia. There are a total of 29 municipalities with 29 presidents who were elected in keeping with legal regulations. They were elected by municipal assemblies or whenever there were municipal councils, and this applied to areas in which no elections were held, or perhaps incomplete elections. In those cases, a Municipal Council would step in, which was a council appointed by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know the names of the heads of districts, and what were the districts, specifically?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I know. I did work with those people, didn't I? There was the Kosovo district in Pristina, Veljko Odalovic was head; the Pec district, headed by Jovo Popovic; the Kosovska Mitrovica district, headed by a number of different people. They took turns; Prizren district, headed by Brankica Furijanovic; and then the Gnjilane district, headed by Mr. Kovacevic. As for the municipalities, I know the names of most of their representatives, especially those with whom I was in close contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Give us five or six.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Pec, Jovo Ivanovic; Pristina, Dusan Simic; and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your activities on the ground, you talked about the operation concerning the implementation of the regulations and policies of the government of the Republic of Serbia. You were in touch with most of the ministries; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Which ministries, specifically, and why?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, specifically, the Ministry of Finance funding the work of the municipalities, a shortage of funds which was particularly prominent in some of the municipalities because of their special needs, needs that had not been envisioned in the municipal budget, that had not been provided for. There were interventions in certain companies in such municipalities where this was needed. The Ministry of Agriculture --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: One thing at a time, please. What about some of the ministers and deputy ministers, did they not travel to Pristina every once in awhile and then fly back? And were some of them there all the time, and who were those ministers and deputy ministers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Most often, the Minister of Agriculture was in Kosovo, Mr. Babovic; then the federal Minister for Internal Trade, Mr. Miskovic; then the Minister of Justice would come, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of Serbia. It was only that one. Well, then the Minister of Health, Mrs. Leposava Milicevic, came. As for those who were permanently stationed and were in my headquarters, or rather, in my team, that was the assistant Minister for Labour and Social Matters, Mr. Tomislav Kujundzic; and the assistant Minister for Agriculture, Mr. Slobodan Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about Health?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: For Health, yes, he was there, too. Well, he was also operational in the field. All of us who were down there were most often in the municipalities where there were problems that had been manifested.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you were sent down there, you established this headquarters, this outpost. What do we call it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was staying at the provincial authority's premises with these three men who had been assigned to me, and I operated from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you went to municipalities often and that you had contacts with all the five heads of districts and 29 municipalities, and you said a few moments ago that you particularly went to the municipalities where there were problems.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You established an outpost of the government of the Republic of Serbia, if I understood you correctly. You were appointed coordinator.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It cannot be said that this was a special outpost.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters cannot hear Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were people who helped me in carrying out my work. I sent them, of course, to different municipalities so that certain problems would be eliminated, problems that had cropped up there. My method of work was to have meetings held from time to time with all the presidents and heads, and especially sometimes in the districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were the special problems that you resolved on the ground; that is to say, in these districts, municipalities, and so on? Try to remember a few of them, a few types.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The problems were different. They varied from one municipality to another. Somewhere it was the health services that functioned poorly, then problems in education, problems in the work of the courts. There were many cases and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Unresolved?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, unresolved. What cases should be given priority, and so on; then the functioning of local self-government, lack of water in individual municipalities, settlements. There were other issues, too, related to the functioning of the economy because we were making an effort to have everything work in the conditions that were as they were. I can say that most companies -- or rather, all companies, except for a smaller number, did work while I was down there in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. I think that we do get the picture in terms of what your tasks were in Kosovo and Metohija as coordinator of the government of the state of Serbia. So would you agree with me that you were simply in charge of making life happen as normally as possible?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was in charge of making it possible for all institutions to function and to have a normal life set up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now let us go back to why we are actually meeting here. Were there problems in your work in relation to the situation that prevailed in Kosovo in these complications? I shouldn't say the whole thing my, because the situation was not quite normal, was it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. There was a special state of fear among people. Many roads had been closed down; for example, just to give you a few examples, Orahovac-Pristina via Malisevo; then Decani-Djakovica; in the Kosovska Mitrovica district, it was Srbica-Glogovac; and so on. People, the presidents of the municipalities and other people out on the ground, were stating that there were these difficulties, and people were afraid, panic-stricken. They were in a situation in which they were looking for a solution in order to normalise the situation, to ensure unhindered movement, life, and work, not to have any fear present. And there was fear, no doubt about that. That was what the situation was. Even while I was there, killings had started here and there; then the open-face mine that was the artery for providing coal to the coal-fired power plants; then - what was the name? - Bilacevac, yes, near Pristina. And it is only natural that people made these demands. I conveyed this to the prime minister; that is to say, an impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sorry, we'll get to that. Are you aware of the existence of the KLA in the period while you were there; that is, June-September 1998? What can you tell us about the activities of this organisation and the consequences of their activity?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I did not deal with that particular subject matter. But since I was there, I have eyes and ears, so I heard things and I even saw some things. They, the KLA, carried out attacks here and there in different places. They kidnapped and even killed people. No doubt about that. I was informed about that, among other things, when I talked to presidents of municipalities and people and citizens in villages and towns where I went. So I can say --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Could you please now look at the letter that is right in front of you, and tell us what this is, what you have before you. Who kind this, and what is this all about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a letter, a warning, whatever you wish to call it, addressed by the president of the municipality of Orahovac, Mr. Andjelko Kolasinac, in which he warns that every day the terrorists are moving the lines closer and closer to Orahovac, Velika Hoca, Zociste, and Opterusa; and, in fact, they encircled these settlements. He is saying that the civilian population is running out of patients because of day-to-day provocations by Albanian terrorists by firearms. In this document, he appeals and hopes that the security forces will resolve this problem, but, obviously, we can see in the text of the letter that even he is losing hope. And he says here that there may even be some self-organisation. Because if that would not happen, there would be an exodus of the Serb people from that area or occupation by the KLA. He --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In that paragraph where he says, "in order to prevent the worst -- "In view of this, and in order to avoid the worst," does Mr. Kolasinac think it is a bad solution if the population were to organise themselves? What does he mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that calls for speculation on the part of this witness as phrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's right, Mr. Fila. I think that can be asked possibly of the witness and his own concern, but it's really not for him to interpret these words. This letter wasn't addressed to him, for example. It was addressed to other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at this down here, it says: "To the government of the Republic of Serbia." He's the Republic of Serbia. He's the government. It was submitted to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to hear that from the witness rather than Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, did you receive this letter in your capacity as coordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received this letter, and I personally talked to Mr. Kolasinac, the president of the municipality of Orahovac, because right after that he came to see me in Pristina, and he presented the whole problem to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, in that case it is -- in that case, it is open to you to ask, to expand upon the comment in the letter, if you can, by asking appropriate questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, please carefully read the paragraph - one, two, three, four - five. It says: "In view of this, and in order to avoid the worst, people organising on their own initiative ..." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
