utterances.text: That means that the Serb people would oppose such things happening. Of course, that did not happen, because the position of the state was that things could not be done that way but, rather, only through appropriate organs that were established for that in accordance with the law and constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Kolasinac personally present this position to you, that he believed that this was the worst solution?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he said. That is the settlement that is there. And, indeed, from all sides, nearby, there were terrorist centres according to what people said; and then Suva Reka, Malisevo, Ostrozub, Dragobilje were nearby and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In that same sentence, Mr. Kolasinac says the following: "We appeal for organised protection by our state, the Republic of Serbia." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: He's asking to be protected, Orahovac and the other settlements, in regular ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And, finally, in the last paragraph, he says: "We hope that we will speedily receive assistance in the form of certain protection forces before it is too late."

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In that letter, he expresses his fear of an exodus by the population.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, a few moments ago we were saying that it was your obligation to inform Prime Minister Marjanovic about what you found out about as you were travelling and carrying out your coordinating duties. On the basis of this letter and other letters, if there were other letters as well, did you inform Mr. Marjanovic about that, and perhaps someone else as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: About this letter, I informed Mr. Marjanovic; however, he told me that he had received the letter and that all measures would be taken, and that I should convey that to Kolasinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I only informed Marjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, it is generally known - and I hope there will be no objections that I'm leading you - that at that time there was a large group of foreign diplomats present in Kosovo and Metohija, representatives of states and governments, international organisations, humanitarian organisations, and so on and so forth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I'm interested in now is the following: Did you meet with any of them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marjanovic, the prime minister, instructed me subsequently, in terms of Kosovo and Metohija -- or rather, Pristina, to talk to diplomats there, to representatives of humanitarian and non-governmental organisations, and that started from as early as mid-June. I can say --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, before we move on to specific persons, what kind of organisations were there, from what countries, that you came across? We'll deal with them individually later.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In Kosovo and Metohija, there were numerous humanitarian organisations. I can only enumerate the most influential ones. These were the International Committee of the Red Cross, the UNHCR, various other humanitarian organisations which were active there providing aid to the population all over Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Apart from these humanitarian and other organisations, apart from the ones you enumerated, did you have meetings with diplomats and ambassadors of foreign countries who were not involved in humanitarian issues?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had numerous meetings. Let me mention but a few. I talked to Mr. Satak, the deputy Secretary of State of the USA. There was a ten-member team; on two occasions with the deputy Foreign Minister of Russia, Mr. Afasanijevski.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Afasanijevski, yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Then I spoke to representatives of the OSCE; to representatives of the European Union; to the ambassadors of England, Germany, France, Italy; numerous representatives stationed there; and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does the name of Mr. Dinsberg, Mr. Petritsch, Mr. Pedersen mean anything to you? Did you have meetings with them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met Mr. Petritsch as many as three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: There were high-ranking representatives of humanitarian organisations, human rights representatives: Margaret O'Keefe, Sadako Ogata, Beatrice Weber, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Ms. Sadako Ogata was from the UN Committee for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There were three or four delegations a day. What was Mrs. Elizabeth Rehn?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: She was representing the UN on human rights issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We will have some questions about what they were interested in. First of all, what were they interested in, in connection with the measures concerning citizens when they spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: They were all interested in how the Moscow declaration was being implemented. The two presidents, Mr. Yeltsin and Mr. Milosevic, had signed it, and they weren't just interested in as it relates to my sphere of activity; that is, whether displaced persons were returning to their hearths and homes, whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You'll have to slow down.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: -- whether foodstuffs and other necessities were being provided, medicines and other necessities, what activities were being carried out to repair houses which had been damaged or destroyed, what measures had been adopted or were being planned by the government of the Republic of Serbia with a view to resolving these issues; and other issues as well, for example, something that was not within my competence but it was mentioned by other diplomats.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they ask for freedom of movement of diplomatic representatives and representatives of humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They never failed to mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And that was within the scope of the Moscow declaration?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It may be interesting to say what I said to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that. But to all those questions that were being put, do you know that apart from the Moscow declarations there were certain demands being made by the OSCE, the European Union, the Contact Group, and others? Did they mention those in their talks with you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These demands were of a similar nature, that necessary aid should be provided to people, that humanitarian organisations should be allowed free movement, as should diplomatic representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. We have heard what they asked. Now will you tell us what you told them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I informed them in detail of the measures being taken by the government of the Republic of Serbia in order to provide for the normal life and work of the population in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you tell them anything about humanitarian aid and who it was being provided to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was being sent especially to the areas that were at risk and to Kosovo and Metohija. In high-risk areas, we delivered food, supplies for personal hygiene, materials for the repair of damaged houses. I told them that we were making it possible for refugees to return to their homes. We were providing them with free transportation. And the government of the Republic of Serbia more than once publicly expressed its standpoint that people should go back to their hearths and homes, and this was being done, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: There was any discrimination when humanitarian aid was being distributed? Was it, for example, given to members of the SPS or to Serbs only?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no discrimination at all. I visited those areas, and I did not see any discrimination. Had I seen it, I would have protested vehemently. Those were my instructions, and I would also have done it because I'm human, but those were my instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SPS?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You became a member of the government as a non-party person?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you tell them that the government of Serbia was providing free passage?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, especially in the case of humanitarian organisations. They were the ones who spoke to me more. The diplomats only did so in formal talks. But we invested enormous efforts to make sure that the humanitarian aid that arrived from any organisation should reach its destined goal. Sometimes there were hitches, sometimes it would be held up for a few hours, but we always managed to remove any obstacles through the competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you acquaint the foreign diplomats and representatives of the humanitarian organisations with the problems you spoke about earlier, in connection with the letter by Mr. Kolasinac, about persons who were kidnapped or imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That was not my task. As regards the security situation, that was not my task; but, in my conversations, of course, I did mention terrorist activities in general. But as regards the persons who had been kidnapped or abducted, I regularly mentioned that even if they didn't ask me about it, because that was a very problem. I did not think when I went to visit Kosovo and Metohija that that would be a major preoccupation of mine; however, it became that as a result of the onslaught, so to speak, of the parents and relatives of persons who had been kidnapped or abducted. There were 2 or 300 such cases while I was there; and in various places, I had over ten meetings. These were very unpleasant conversations, because those relatives went so far as to issue threats. They said, "If they can kidnap my father, my brother, my son, why don't you let us do the same?" And I told them that the official organs were doing their job, that I was telling all this to the foreign diplomats and humanitarian representatives who were there, and that they were all promising that the problem would be solved. However, it always came to nothing, their promises.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. So the result of all your talks was meager. Nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no results because none of these people ever came back, and only now has it come to light or is it coming to light that they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We'll now talk about humanitarian aid, because that's an issue here. You said more than once that you were involved in creating the conditions for humanitarian aid to reach its goal. How was this done? What did this look like?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the humanitarian organisations brought aid in large quantities. I think a lot of effort was invested by them, but we also, as the government of the Republic of Serbia, and others, for example, companies and others, brought in aid. It was our wish that all areas where aid was needed be covered, and the humanitarian organisations also were concerned about that, especially the ICRC and the UNHCR. We harmonised our work with them. When distributing aid, if there were temporarily displaced persons, especially in inaccessible places, the problems were more serious. There were places where we couldn't go, and then the humanitarian organisations took aid to those places. They took the most necessary things there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I didn't understand. When you were unable to act, they did. What does that mean? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were certain areas where objectively, because of the terrorists, we could not go; for example, Djeravica towards the border with Albania. It's up in the mountains above Junik. At the end of June, there was a group there. It was established that there were 2 or 3.000 people there, but there were about 300 in fact. And for three days, we negotiated with the UNHCR and Mr. Vargas who persistently wanted aid to be taken there. Well, we wanted that also. It was our proposal, for reasons of security, that it should go via Decani, but he insisted it should go via Junik for reasons of his own. And in the end, simply to make sure that those people received aid, we said, "All right, go via Junik." But we could not guarantee freedom of movement there because at that time that area was, so to say, occupied by the terrorists. It was under their control, to put it quite simply. There were other areas as well. At a later stage, we set up humanitarian centres in the areas most at risk, in the municipalities. And we even agreed with some of the humanitarian organisations that they should inject part of their goods into these humanitarian centres, and this was very good for the restoration of confidence and for bringing people closer together, because in those centres it everybody received aid, Serbs, Albanians, Turks, Roma. And the humanitarian centre in Orahovac was especially successful. It was visited more than once by foreign diplomatic representatives and delegations. I visited it two or three times, and I can say that it worked really well. They provided glass for windows that had been shattered in the terrorist and anti-terrorist activities, building materials for the repair of houses, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you inform those organisations of the fact that we were having problems with kidnapped persons? And were only Serbs kidnapped or were there others as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I informed everybody. That was what I was supposed to do, and I believed it necessary to do just that, to talk to everyone and tell them about these problems and to try to do something about the problems, in the hope of bringing someone back at least, so that hope might be given to others, too. Unfortunately, everybody agreed that the problem was there, that it was quite a pronounced problem and a painful one in purely human terms. We even went as far as to offer an exchange to be organised through the mediation of diplomats who would have been in a position to deal with the other side; however, we weren't successful in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Everything that you've been telling us about, all these things, who was it that you informed about these things?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: My line of reporting went straight to the prime minister of the Republic of Serbia and him alone. As for humanitarian issues, I would sometimes inform our commission, the republican Commission for Refugees, which existed at the time and operated. In Kosovo and Metohija, there were refugees from the Krajina region and Bosnia, about 13.000 of those, if I remember correctly, and some of those were facing great hardship, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In view of the situation as you have described it for us, was a body set up to assist those citizens of Kosovo who were at risk, whose situation was precarious at the time, in terms of providing them with supplies?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact how complex the distribution of supplies was to people in Kosovo and Metohija, at the level of the Republic of Serbia, headquarters were set up for distributing supplies to the people in Kosovo and Metohija. In parallel, a provincial centre was set up as well as supply centres throughout the districts and municipalities. As for the republican headquarters, there was the Minister for Domestic Trade of Yugoslavia, Mr. Miskovic; the Minister of Agriculture of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Babovic; some deputy ministers; and from Kosovo, we had Ratko Jocic, who was president of the supply centre in Kosovo and Metohija. The presidents throughout the districts were the head of districts; and in municipalities, the presidents of the respective municipalities. The headquarters had the task of making sure that there would be sufficient supplies to distribute throughout Kosovo and Metohija. I, too, was involved in the work of the headquarters, the central office, so to speak, and we had three different aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the headquarters? Were there people there involved with health, with construction, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Deputies or assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Deputy or assistant ministers, you mean?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You were involved in the work of the headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the central office. But whenever I could, I also went to meetings of the provincial headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where were the meetings held?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In Pristina, those of the central office. Sometimes two or three times there were meetings in Belgrade, and sometimes in the various districts depending on the problems that arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the principal objective of the headquarters at the central office?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: To make sure there were sufficient supplies for a normal life and to keep everything operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Which supplies, specifically?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Foodstuffs above all; specifically, flour, oil, sugar, meat. The basic necessities; potatoes, beans, that sort of thing. The basic necessities to feed people. Also --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. And these were distributed, too, to everyone alike?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was for the entire population. Humanitarian aid was distributed free of charge. These were human rights supplies as they called them, and special funds were set apart for that, and special supplies within the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What types of supplies were there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: We had three different types: Humanitarian supplies, free of charge, and this sort was dispatched to areas that were at risk and distributed to refugees, people who were without their homes provisionally, and also to those who were socially disenfranchised. There were the so-called intervention shipments, and these dealt with supplies that did not abound at the time. That's what everybody needed: Oil, beans, flour, meat, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So who did that go to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: These shipments used the normal routes used by goods for the purposes of trade, but these commodities were sometimes taken from the state reserves. So there had to be an intervention, in a manner of speaking, by the state to supplement these supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the third type?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: And the third type was commercial supplies, commercial supplies following the mechanisms of the market. However, the important thing here was the whole thing was organised. The state took matters into its own hands in order to avoid shady situations which sometimes occur in this sort context. There were companies that were in charge of this, and these companies were closely watched. There were inspection teams monitoring the whole process. There was an agriculture inspection team, there was a health inspection team, and a trade inspection team; the health inspection, because they were dealing with medications, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, there were three aspects to this: The first being humanitarian aid shipments, free for all, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, free for all, everyone alike. All those who were in need: Displaced persons; people in a socially inferior position, and those who had simply run out of food. Food has sometimes gone stale -- gone stale and rotten in people's homes which they had to leave behind because of the operations of the terrorists. That's how it worked. Humanitarian aid shipments were dispatched through these humanitarian aid centres later on, but our Yugoslav Red Cross also was concerned with this, where the state was concerned; then also international humanitarian organisations who had a lot of influence on bringing the supply situation in Kosovo and Metohija back to normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you can confirm that it was distributed to everyone with no discrimination whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. No question about that. All those who were in need.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The other two aspects of supplies, the commercial type, for example, how was that secured? How did you make sure that people got it at the right price, at a fair price?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The whole procedure was closely watched by inspection teams. Very often, the supplies came from the state's commodity reserves, and there were organisations that were authorised to deal with the flow of goods. Payments were made based on these commodity reserves and also to other companies, and this worked smoothly. The danger was looming that the market might be unsettled. Some people, for example, could have taken more of the goods in order to resell them the next day. We stood in the way of this sort of practice, and this greatly enhanced the entire process.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Based on your own assessment on the functioning of these various headquarters from the central office to the ground level, the municipal ones, what would that assessment be?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Everything worked smoothly given the circumstances that prevailed. I'm quite happy with their work. They met their objectives. They met all the goals that they had been established for.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sir, let us dwell on this for a minute. Let us try to zoom in on a detail that we have not discussed so far. We talked about the objections being raised by various diplomats and about how you worked in order to make sure that the state administration worked properly and that humanitarian aid reached its destination. You would agree with me, though, wouldn't you that there was shooting in Kosovo throughout; right? There were all sorts of problems. That's why I'm asking you this. What about these foreign diplomats? When they came to speak to you, and you told us about that, did they ever underline any concerns they might have had about possible crimes in Kosovo? Could you tell us anything about that, sir, regarding any of the sides, not just this side. Not just the KLA.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It is true that these problems, the problems of looting, on all sides, were mentioned. And this was happening throughout Kosovo and Metohija, and this is one of the concerns that were being underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To all practical intents, what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That there was a lot of looting all over the place --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, now --

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: -- that crime was rife throughout the area: Looting, threats being made, incidents, punch-ups, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. To be clear about this, you're being asked about things that foreign diplomats told you. You would surely be aware of these things without a diplomat having to tell you about them, local crime and looting. I don't think that's what Mr. Fila's asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. We have been speaking about the fact that diplomats were asking questions about humanitarian aid and everything else, safe passage, how the agreement was being implemented. So did they tell him anything about what they themselves had learned on the ground in terms of various crimes being committed, such as murder, robbery, looting. Did they ask him to provide information on that sort of thing. That's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they at any point tell you about this, and did they seek information from you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a particularly leading question you've asked, and it must inevitably affect the value of the answer, but let's hear what the witness can tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to hurry things along.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter did not understand Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said my apologies for this leading question. However, the way the trial has been going so far, it was clear that this would happen. All I'm trying to do is to economise in terms of time. Let's try again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can't let that go without commenting. There is no reason why the way in which the trial has been going should lead to unnecessary leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. My apologies then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During those talks, in addition to safe passage, unrestricted access, and humanitarian aid, were there any other subjects being raised by these diplomats in terms of what was happening in Kosovo throughout your time there, the period between June and September?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: They wanted to know about a whole lot of different things. I was in charge of certain things and I knew about certain things, and those were the subjects that I discussed with them, and I provided specific answers. There were questions raised sometimes in relation to which I was unable to provide complete answers. Specifically, when talking about displaced persons, humanitarian aid, unrestricted movement, distribution of humanitarian aid, kidnappings, abductions, there were permanent answers being provided and requests by me for them to help us deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about beyond all of this? Did they notice anything else? Did they enjoy unrestricted movement throughout Kosovo and Metohija, humanitarian organisations and diplomats alike?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unrestricted movement was guaranteed and security to diplomats and humanitarian organisations. On the whole I think I can say that I think this worked well. There were sporadic problems, needless to say, but my general assessment would be that things worked smoothly in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Did they warn you at any point? Did they inform you? Did they tell you that anything was happening that wasn't good, that anything was happening that would run counter to the normal functioning of a country?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: My talks with them went in all sorts of directions. They asked their own questions. What they wanted to know, I answered. We discussed all sorts of issues. Of course, that's the sort of talks that we had. And given the sort of problems that were there, there were different kinds of questions being raised. Some asked questions about this and some about that. I talked about matters of general interest, and this is the sort of thing that I normally told them about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did they ever mention the fact that, as they were moving about, they actually noticed specific crimes being committed, such as, for example, looting, murder, perhaps? Did they tell you anything about that? Did they seek information from you about any of these things?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. He's hinted about murders three times now, and he hasn't got the answer yet. I think anything he gets now is not going to helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think, in view of the way he has approached it so far, he's entitled to be more specific, Mr. Hannis. So let's hear the answer is to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were such questions; namely, that looting should be prevented, improper conduct. That was absolutely the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that the question?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It was the answer, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just slow down. Sir, could you just wait a second. Wait for the letters to stop appearing on the screen, and then start answering. You told us that there were such questions. Right. Now, my question is as follows - wait for it to come out and then this answer - what did you do, if anything, in order to check such claims? Was that really going on, these things that they were telling you about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I expressed my interest. I expressed my interest through my own lines of communication; that is to say, through presidents of municipalities and others. And I can say that there were various gangs that were involved in stealing, looting, also some more serious things in terms of jeopardising the property, safety of citizens. Usually, it was village gangs that were at each other's throats, and that was dealt with judiciously. I was telling people, I was saying, "People, see to this, see that it is eliminated, that this goes away."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you ask the five district heads?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I did. I asked them, too. I can also say that I talked to --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Slowly, slowly answer my questions. You -- your answer was that you asked them, too, then?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sir, what was their reply to you when you asked them? Did this kind of thing happen in their districts, the things that we've been talking about -- or rather, that foreign representatives talked about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Their reply was that there were such individual cases but that these were people from the sphere of crime who tried to take advantage of this difficult situation for their own objectives; that is to say, for attaining their own dishonourable objectives, but that they were held responsible and that they were handed over to relevant prosecution authorities; most of them, that is, as many as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The building where you stayed in Pristina, was the army there or the police or who was in that building? The building where those headquarters of yours were.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I lived in the corps building.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What corps?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the corps of the army of Yugoslavia; the 3rd Corps, the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just take it slowly. While you stayed there, did you come across military men, and who was it at that, if you saw them at all.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Since I lived, there I encountered officers, commissioned and non-commissioned; and in the immediate vicinity, there was internal affairs, too, so I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Slowly. I'm asking you about officers.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you know who the commander of the 3rd Army was at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: When I was there, General Samardzic was commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see him, too?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I encountered him two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, as for General Samardzic, did you ask him about this information that you were receiving from diplomats, what we've been discussing so far? Now, slowly. So I mean about what was going on in the field, things that run counter to criminal codes. And if you asked him about these things, can you tell us what it was that he answered?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: He expressed his interest by the way in the work that I was dealing with, and then we discussed broader subjects as well, including these issues even. We had similar assessments, almost identical assessments; namely, that such things were happening and that this should be prevented energetically, which was indeed being done within the scope of the possibilities that existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, the building that you lived in, was that perhaps the military hotel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I lived at the corps. Well, yes, other officers lived there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So is this building the corps building or the military hotel building?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's a military hotel, and then the corps was nearby, staying right there, nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At this hotel?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It's not a hotel. It's the corps building, a big building. I lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In that building?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And others?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Other officers lived there, too. And the commander of the corps lived there in that building as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And near you, near your building, near this building where you lived, regardless of whether it's a hotel or the corps or whatever, was there a police headquarters there? Let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In the immediate vicinity, there was the MUP building. I don't know exactly how many metres away, but it wasn't far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Did you encounter members of the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, did you ask them, too -- or rather, did you talk to them, too, in order to obtain information or to check what the foreign diplomats were telling you about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I talked to them as well. I also had policemen from the area where I was born. So I asked them about the situation there, and they were telling me that such things were happening, but they didn't have any special information because everybody there was doing their own work. And it is only natural that these crimes had been registered, and they were reported in order for proceedings to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. As for these objection raised by diplomats and foreigners, and as for the results of your own investigations, if I can call it that way, your talks with the heads of districts and the presidents of municipalities, did you inform Prime Minister Marjanovic about that, and someone else perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As for this, as well as other matters, I informed the prime minister, Mirko Marjanovic, only, because that is what has been agreed upon; although, I should say quite only, that this was not my own line of work, and this was not the subject matter that I dealt with. But I thought it was serious problem, and I thought I should inform the prime minister in order for appropriate measures to be tank. I did not talk to others, and it was not my own like of work, but I assume -- well, everybody has their own work and is in charge of the work he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did Mr. Marjanovic say to you, if anything, when you reported about these things and the results that you had reached, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Prime Minister Marjanovic said to me that I should particularly pay attention to the work that I was in charge of; and in addition to that, if I have any other information, it would be well come because it can assist the work of other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Now, let us go back to your own work now. Could you describe to us what this humanitarian situation in Kosovo and Metohija was like? But before you start answering, could you please look at 2D3382. Study it slowly, and then we'll discuss it. 2D382 is the number, actually. It's the last document.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you. Can you -- what is this? What document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Wait a minute. All right. In the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a press statement of the Secretary for Information of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, dated the 27th of August, 1999. After talks were conducted by Mr. Veljko Odalovic, the chief of the Kosovo district, and myself, with the assistant of the Secretary of State to the United States of America, Mrs. Taft, and the chief of the American mission in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Richard Miles?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: -- Mr. Richard Miles, who were visiting Kosovo and Metohija with their associates, on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what does paragraph 2 indicate?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 indicates --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Slowly, slowly.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 indicates that: "As per the resolution of humanitarian questions, what is expected is the full engagement of international humanitarian organisations ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Slowly.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: -- "... and that with the help of the Yugoslav Red Cross and state organs, they need to support all the efforts made by the Republic of Serbia in this area."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the assessment of the work done to date?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It was emphasised that cooperation to date had been good.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see in the transcript, the answer refers it as being a document the 27th of August, 1999. I know the English translation says 1999, but my B/C/S version says 1998, and I think we need to clear up which year we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was assuming the B/C/S was the accurate document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eight. 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it is 1998. It's fairly obvious it couldn't be 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wouldn't have spoken except the answer got translated as 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How was the cooperation to date assessed? Wait. Wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That question has already been answered, and you --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, all right, is sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- were proceeding to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, what is it that you emphasised there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, I pointed out that, in accordance with the Moscow declaration by Presidents Milosevic and Yeltsin, free movement was made possible for all diplomatic and humanitarian missions in all directions in Kosovo and Metohija, and that all problems that might arise were being eliminated through intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what did you express then?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I also informed the American diplomats about the establishment of 11 humanitarian posts in the territory of the province up until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you stress the problem of the abducted?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me -- yes. I stressed the problem of citizens who had been abducted by terrorists, and I expressed great dissatisfaction with the resolving of those problems, and I asked for a new assistance and cooperation of all, including international humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about Mr. Odalovic, Chief Odalovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: He talked about activities and measures that the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were taking so that the civilian population, which had, due to terrorist activity as well as various separatist groups and gangs, been forced to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what was asked for? What was explained? What were the state organs doing?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: State organs were doing -- were taking all measures in order to take care of the population, to provide construction material, food supplies, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Last question from this set of questions is whether these diplomats had any objections in respect of any of the things you asserted, or did they accept it that way at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there weren't any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this would be an appropriate moment in view of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, we have to break again at this stage. This time for half an hour. Would you please go with the usher. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 10 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we were told that the system is down. That's why I was not dressed on time, and my colleagues are telling me I cannot work, but I don't understand anything about these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you and I together will be good enough to take them on, Mr. Fila. The question is whether we need it at any stage, and that will depend on how the exhibits are to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you've dealt with your exhibits now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You have looked at that exhibit. We won't need it any more. Now I will ask you, based on what you have read and everything you have said so far, to give us an overview of the humanitarian situation in Kosovo and Metohija throughout the period of your stay there, June 1998 to September 1998, an overview by municipality.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The humanitarian situation in Kosovo and Metohija existed from the first to the last day. These problems were solved successfully in spite of certain difficulties; however, a general assessment might be that the problems were solved successfully. They were so successful owing to the concern of the government of Serbia, the municipal organs, and other organs as well as companies, which provided necessities, staple foods, building materials. And let me point out that a vast amount of help arrived from international humanitarian organisations, which, as far as I could tell - and I did participate in those talks and in all the work that went on - made a huge contribution to solving these problems. We managed to improve the situation in terms of organisation also. Because at a certain stage, we established humanitarian centres in the municipalities and villages which were most at risk. Up to September, 14, these had been established, and I visited these humanitarian centres; that is, the ones in Orahovac, Decani, Klina, Djakovica, and also in some villages. There was one in Junik, one in Istinic, and so on, and I've already mentioned Orahovac. In my view, these were very good places, because goods, foodstuffs, building materials, glass for windows was received there by all citizens. I visited the one in Orahovac, and there was one person from the Red Cross, one from the centre for social work. And we did our best to have people from the local self-administration there, both Serbs and Albanians wherever possible; for example, in Orahovac, it worked really well. I was there one day when humanitarian aid was being distributed to all citizens, including Roma, Albanians, Serbs, and others. They took glass panes for glazing their houses. They took foodstuffs, everything they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was the humanitarian situation the same in municipalities where there was no KLA activity as in those where there was such activity?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The humanitarian situation in the municipalities where there were no terrorist activities practically did not exist. Aid was distributed to those citizens who had arrived there, moved there on a temporary basis because they were displaced; otherwise, part of Kosovo functioned normally. In places where, there were many displaced persons accommodated, and they were mostly concentrated in towns. There was some in Montenegro, and a small number in Albania. That's the displaced persons who had been driven away from their hearth and home because of terrorist activity. And I can even say that in areas under KLA control, even there humanitarian aid was delivered. For the most part, most of these international humanitarian organisations did that; and here and there, it was our Red Cross working on that task. There were enough goods. The commodity reserves always intervened when it was impossible to get goods from other sources. And it's also interesting to mention, with respect to these humanitarian centres, that international humanitarian organisations participated in those with some of their goods. And this was very good for confidence building, helping people understand that things were changing for the better. And I have to say that, in September, the situation was consolidated to a great extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be a summary of your stay there as regards humanitarian issues while you were in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. One can't go into every detail. There would be a lot of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, maybe you could write your memoirs. Every general before this Court has written at least one book?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, that's not true. General Naumann has not written a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, now let's move on, and we will talk about Mr. Sainovic. That will be our last topic. Do you know Mr. Sainovic? Since when have you known him, and what do you know about him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I have known Mr. Sainovic since the 1980s. He worked in the mining and foundry complex in Bor, and he was one of the leaders there, one of the head people. He was also the president of Bor municipality, and I was president of a neighbouring municipality, Zagubica. We cooperated very often because many people from my municipality, which was very poor, worked in the Bor basin. Also, I knew Mr. Sainovic and continued cooperating with him after he went to Belgrade, where he became Minister of Mining and Energy. And in the 1990s, he was also the prime minister of the Republic of Serbia. Later on, he was deputy prime minister of the federal government, and I knew him then also because we worked together on certain tasks of common interest for our native area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic -- in Kosovo and Metohija in the course of the 1980s, when you were there, did you see Mr. Sainovic there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would see Mr. Sainovic in Kosovo in the period from July, early July, approximately, to the end of September when I left Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you meet him there? Did you know what he was doing there? How did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I met him in Pristina in early July 1998, and I was told that he was coming to Kosovo and Metohija by the prime minister. Several days before his arrival, the prime minister told me that Mr. Sainovic was coming to Kosovo, and that I should apply to him whenever I was dealing with the foreign affairs or talks with diplomats, because he had been delegated to be in charge of those tasks by the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an error in the transcript. There's an error in the transcript. It says 1980; it should say 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's been corrected. Which prime minister told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The prime minister of Serbia. My prime minister who delegated me. He told me that on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What do you know about Nikola Sainovic's tasks while he was in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: He told me this himself, and I also learned it from the prime minister of the Republic of Serbia. He was in charge of foreign policy, of talks with foreign diplomatic representatives in Kosovo and Metohija. He was in charge of coordinating all that, because I have to say, and I've already pointed this out, at that time there were numerous diplomats in Kosovo and Metohija. The place was teeming with various ambassadors, ministers, diplomats, lower-ranking diplomats, various missions from the European Union. There was the European troika.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you who were there and the local authorities, were you able to deal with foreign policy affairs independently?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Before going to Kosovo and Metohija, as a municipal president, I had had the opportunity of meeting several ambassadors, but I didn't have much experience with foreign diplomats. So, when in Kosovo and Metohija, I was tasked with talking to foreign diplomats on various issues. This was quite difficult for me, so I welcomed the arrival of Mr. Sainovic, as we were acquaintances. I found this very useful, and I took the liberty of asking him to tell me about his experiences in that area, and I can tell you that I welcomed his assistance in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could one say that you exchanged information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. I told him about the work I was doing, so that he could make use of what I told him in his talks that he held. I asked him to help me concerning certain issues. I was insufficiently familiar with, I didn't understand sufficiently, and this helped me in those conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During your stay in Kosovo, June, July, August, and September, did you hear any mention of a body called a "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. While I was in Kosovo and Metohija, I never heard the term. Later on, when the trial of Milosevic began, I read that somewhere in the papers, in the press, and I heard it in various conversations. People asked me what it was, and I would say, "Well, I don't know." I'd never heard of it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know that in Kosovo and Metohija, in the summer of 1998, there were also some representatives of the Socialist Party of Serbia, that there were various state and political structures there, and that they had joint meetings?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. On behalf of the Socialist Party of Serbia - I am not sure precisely when, but I think around mid-July - a three-member team arrived: Milomir Minic, Dusan Matkovic, and Andjelovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Zoran Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were in the SPS building, but they also used the premises of the regional organs for certain talks they had with various structures and with citizens. I know that Dusan Matkovic was tasked with helping the economy by making suggestion and so on, because he was the managing director of Sartid in Smederevo, and he had a lot of experience in that area. And in view of some work I had done on the economy in Kosovo and Metohija, I worked in coordination with him. We discussed certain issues of personnel, especially when there were companies that were in difficulties of any kind, whether financial difficulties or difficulties in production. I know that Zoran Andjelkovic was a party activist who travelled a lot on the ground, and he also received certain parties for talks. As for Milomir Minic, he dealt with party work. He held meetings, attended meetings, consultations and so on, and he was there, too. They worked both in the SPS building and in the regional premises where they received people who came to see them. I also saw other representatives at meetings held now and then in these buildings. There were also individual representatives of the state organs such as --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you attend any such meetings?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not attend such meetings, because my method of work was mostly visiting on the ground. I had my own methods and my own ways of getting information, so I felt no need of attending such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sainovic have any influence on your work as the coordinator of the work of state organs, or did you influence his work?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Neither did he influence my work, nor did I influence his. We cooperated as colleagues. We consulted one another. We had coffee together. We had drinks together. We may even have had lunch once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You told us that back in 1998 you saw certain military and police officers there. Do you know what it looked like back in 1998? How was the army being commanded, and what about the police, and who was in charge of what?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not privy to any detail, but I happen to be a reserve officer myself, and I know that the command in the army of Yugoslavia was strictly in keeping with the chain of command. There was strict observance of orders from superiors at their respective levels, and the same things applies to the police force. As it happens, the Minister of the Interior, Zlatko [as interpreted] Stojiljkovic, happens to be from my native area. We hail from the same area, and we talked about things sometimes, and once he told me that they were making sure in the police force that there was strict observance of the chain of command from him on down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My last question to you, Mr. Milosavljevic. You may be -- you might as well start speaking very fast now, this being the last question. I won't be getting at you for that. Can you tell us something about Sainovic as a politician and an economist, since you've known him for quite a long time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: This sort of thing is difficult to put in words, but I think he's an excellent businessman, an excellent economist. As for him as a politician, I find it difficult to say anything about that, but I think he did a good job on the whole. Sainovic is a person who throughout his career, throughout his life, made intense efforts in all sorts of things. He wanted to create new companies, to employ people, to create new jobs because there was always a need for something like that to be done. He was highly regarded in his native area and anywhere he worked, and any elections would show that. He would always -- his name was always on the list. He was always nominated. And wherever he happened to be, the results were always exceptional. The mining and foundry complex of Bor was a huge enterprise, and he earned the respect of everyone, simple workers and leaders alike. He was a man of principle, hard working, honourable. In my view, the kind of person you would like to keep as a friend and you would like to be near.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were his views on a solution for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I talked to him on a number of occasions in Bor and Zagubica, and in Belgrade, too. I know that when he came to Kosovo and Metohija, he advocated a solution by political means. He also advocated the use of the best international and world standards. He said anything should be done to keep the future solution within those perimeters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry for slowing you down all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now give the floor to my colleagues and the OTP. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Line 3, the Minister of Interior, it's not "Zlatko" but "Vlajko." I believe the witness said "Vlajko."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosavljevic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I did say "Vlajko." I may have misspoken. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's fine. That's fine, sir. I said good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. I didn't get it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, you say that you were a minister in the government of the Republic of Serbia between 1994 and 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The government of the Republic of Serbia, can you tell me this: There were sessions every Sunday, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Normally, once a week. Sometimes, whenever the need arose, there were more sessions than just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These were on Thursdays for the most part?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one a week. But as a rule, it would be a Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're concerned about the transcript, it's been clarified now that the meetings are on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosavljevic, there was a stenographic record drawn up of each of the government sessions, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I never wondered about that. I'm not into these technical aspects, but I know that there was always a stenographic record, and there should be one on each and every one of these government meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, in March 1998 - and we looked at 2D356. This is a document appointing you as coordinator in Kosovo and Metohija - the decision was adopted by Prime Minister Marjanovic. According to that document, if I remember correctly - I'm not sure if we could maybe bring this up in e-court - it was your responsibility to report back to the prime minister, and this is something that you told us about, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So your contacts with the government continued even after March 1998, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I was coordinator for the work of state organs and also the president of the Committee for Establishing Damage Caused by Natural Disasters. Until the very end of my term, which was in the year of 2000, I remained president of that committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You often travelled back to Belgrade to attend government sessions throughout your time as coordinator back in 1998, while you were in Kosovo and Metohija, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't travel back that often, but I did go several times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you in touch with the prime minister and the government throughout your time in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. At least once a week, at least. At the very least once a week, I would report back to Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic; sometimes even more frequently by phone. I would give him a ring whenever there was a problem that I needed help one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, do you know that the president of Serbia, Milutinovic, in October 1998, informed the government of the Republic of is Serbia about the contents of the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I read about that in the news papers. I had undergone surgery already at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He was flat on his back at that time, Mr. Zecevic. Can we get to the point of something that he might have some personal experience of?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosavljevic, did you ever see President Milutinovic? Did President Milutinovic attend any of the government sessions that you also attended?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: During my time as a member of the cabinet, Mr. Milutinovic never once attended a government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did another member of the cabinet, at any time, perhaps tell you that President Milutinovic had attended any of the government sessions, apart from the one that I specified in October 1998?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard anything like that; and to be perfectly honest, I didn't ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I do have several questions about this witness's personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, I'm Mihajlo Bakrac, Attorney at Law. I will ask you questions on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. First of all, I will have several questions to ask. But before we start, it would be a good idea for us to look at a short video clip. Please, there is no need for you to pay special attention to the comments made by the journalist. Pay attention to the image itself and what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Defence Exhibit 5D1239.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That was it, Mr. Milosavljevic. Based on this footage, I would like to ask you a couple of questions now. Did you notice yourself in this recording, among other people?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you remember the location of this visit?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: This was in the town of Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this visit occurred?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It occurred in mid-August 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the purpose was for this visit to Malisevo in mid-August 1998?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of my visit, in the presence of the district of the Prizren -- of the president of the Prizren district, Ms. Furjanovic, the mayor of Pristina, and my assistant Toma Kujundzic, whom you can also see in the footage, was to see what the situation was in humanitarian terms in the town of Malisevo. Complaints had been made about the work of the health unit, in terms of the preparations that were being made and in terms of the operations of the health unit. I went to see for myself what the matter was on that day, and I could reassure myself that things were working relatively smoothly. When I say "smoothly," I mean there was humanitarian aid there. It was stationed there in some warehouses and was in the process of being distributed to its users. The health unit at the time had but a single doctor and a nurse had who would travel there occasionally, and yet preparations were being made to set up an entire health station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, one of the OTP's witnesses, Colonel Crosland, in this trial - the transcript reference is 9807, lines 22 and 23 - stated that in July 1998 Malisevo was razed to the ground. So I'm asking you now. You were in Malisevo in August, and we saw that for ourselves. Is it true what Colonel Crosland suggested? Can it be true?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It is certainly not true. What they say where I come from is: Lies or short-lived. You can see in the footage that some minor damage had occurred, but nothing like that. I personally passed through the centre of town. I crossed. Mirusa River. I drank not a single beer. I actually had two beers. It was a particularly hot day, and everybody who was with me felt the same way about the heat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, let me ask you this: Are you aware of the ethnic make-up of the town of Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It was 100 per cent Albanian, which means that the population was 100 per cent Albanian. The town numbers about 10.000 inhabitants. It's a lovely place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And my last question for you: Who was this humanitarian aid for then?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Our citizens. And in this case, they were Albanians, our Albanian population; some of them in Crni Lug. They took advantage of this humanitarian aid as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milosavljevic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sorry, I'm having troubles with my microphone. Let me use this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. You'll forgive me if I don't pronounce your name correctly. I'm having difficulty with it, Mr. Milosavljevic. In one of the questions earlier by Mr. Fila, he asked you if you were a member of the SPS. And your answer was that no, you were not a member of any party. What time period were you talking about when you answered that question?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was talking about when I was chosen to be a minister in the government of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and I was expelled from the party, and then I filed a complaint. When the Socialist Party was formed, then this matter was transferred to the archives. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from when to when were you a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Until October 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And since then you've not been a member of any political party; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe the Defence is back on line, Your Honour, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I had a little explosion of sound in my headphones. Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat it. I didn't hear it because I certainly heard the sound in my headphones, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question was: So, since October 1989, you've not been a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, I became a member of the Yugoslav Left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that is a party that's associated with Slobodan Milosevic's wife, Mrs. Markovic, correct, Mira Markovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: She was a member of that party, too. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you one of the founding members of JUL?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was one of the members. I did not have any high positions in that party. I was a member of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did you cease to be a member of JUL?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I ceased to be a member of JUL in 2000, in the year 2000, towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you heard of an organisation, some sort of honourary commission called "Remembrance and Hope"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll have to check the translation. Maybe my English is not good. So, during the time that you were serving as the coordinator in Kosovo you, were a member of JUL; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you first became a minister in 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That is not right. I became a minister on the 21st of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what were you minister of at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a minister without portfolio in charge of development, reconstruction, and promoting local self-government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who selected you or appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was proposed by the prime minister designate, Mirko Marjanovic, and I was selected by the national assembly of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did you serve in that position?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that. I served a full term from the elections until being relieved from office, for as long as the term of the Serbian Assembly was valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you give me a date for that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Date? I may make a mistake in day or two. The 21st of March, 1994, the 24th of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I also understood that you sort of served as a Minister for Refugees; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was not Minister for Refugees. I was Minister for Religious Affairs from September 1997 until the 24th of March, 1998, because the previous minister had joined the ranks of ambassadors, and then I was supposed to replace him until the term expired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what does the -- what does the Minister for Religious Affairs do?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The Minister for Religious Affairs maintains relations with church organs; carries out administrative work in relation to churches, all denominations; maintains contacts with the representatives of all religious communities; channels from an administrative point various activities in terms of legislative activity, laws, and so on. In order for that to be able to function, I also dealt with issues pertaining to the return of property that had been taken away from the churches in 1945 and after that. Of course, I had these contacts. And during this period of time, I saw the patriarch three times, and several times I met with bishops; mostly with the Bishop of Kragujevac, then the Bishop of Sabac, the Bishop of Pozarevac, the Bishop of Zica, the Bishop of Nis, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you took up those duties, what happened to the work you'd been doing regarding development reconstruction and promoting local self-government. Did you continue to do that job, or did someone take over your old job?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I did both; but in the meantime, a minister for local self-government was established, and I had less work in that area. So I was disburdened, and I could do my work as far as religious affairs was concerned in a more comfortable way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me show you now a document. This is Exhibit P2877. Sir, if you could have a look at this. This relates to a question I asked you earlier, and maybe we can sort out whether it's a translation issue or something else. This is from the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia, and it's from 2000, from the year 2000, and it's a decision on organising the event "Remembrance and Hope."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we may have to go to the bottom of the left-hand column. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Milosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREJA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then if we could go to the top of the right-hand column.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
